paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Pell's equation, also called the Pell–Fermat equation, asks for integers x and y with x² − ny² = 1. Here n is a fixed positive integer that is not a perfect square. Drawn on a graph, the equation is a hyperbola, and each solution is a point on that curve where both coordinates are integers. The plainest one is x = 1 and y = 0, known as the trivial solution.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Joseph Louis Lagrange proved that, whenever n is not a perfect square, the equation has infinitely many different integer solutions. Each solution gives a fraction x/y that is a close approximation to the square root of n. For n = 2, Baudhayana found the solutions x = 17, y = 12 and x = 577, y = 408, and the fractions 17/12 and 577/408 come very close to the square root of 2.

paragraphs.heading: Ancient roots
paragraphs.text: As early as 400 BC, mathematicians in India and Greece studied the numbers coming from the n = 2 case, x² − 2y² = 1, because of its tie to the square root of 2. The Pythagoreans knew the numbers in these approximations as side and diameter numbers. Later, Archimedes approximated the square root of 3 by 1351/780. He did not say how, but that value can be found as a solution to Pell's equation. His cattle problem, about counting the cattle of the sun god Helios, can also be solved by rewriting it as a Pell's equation.

paragraphs.heading: Brahmagupta and Bhāskara II
paragraphs.text: In India, Brahmagupta found an integer solution to 92x² + 1 = y² around 628. His method combined triples: a triple (a, b, k) records numbers with a² − Nb² = k. For N = 92 he composed the triple (10, 1, 8) with itself, divided the result by 64, and composed again to reach the integer solution (1151, 120, 1). In 1150 Bhāskara II gave the first general method that works for every N, called the chakravala, or cyclic, method. At each round it picks, among suitable numbers m, one that makes (m² − N)/k as small as possible, and it always ends with a solution; Bhaskara used it to solve N = 61 with x = 1766319049 and y = 226153980.

paragraphs.heading: Europe and a mistaken name
paragraphs.text: In 1657 Pierre de Fermat, who had found how to solve the equation, set it as a challenge to English mathematicians, naming the cases N = 151 and 313 for John Wallis. Both Wallis and William Brouncker gave solutions, though Wallis hinted in a letter that the answer was Brouncker's. Brouncker was the first European to find a solution. John Pell's link to it was that he revised an English translation of a book that discussed Brouncker's solution. Leonhard Euler wrongly credited that solution to Pell, and that is how the equation got its name.

paragraphs.heading: Lagrange's full theory
paragraphs.text: Lagrange worked out the general theory between 1766 and 1769, using continued fractions and numbers of the form P + Q√a. He proved that the Brouncker–Wallis algorithm always comes to an end. The positive solution with the smallest x is called the fundamental solution. It can always be read off from the sequence of fractions hᵢ/kᵢ, called convergents, of the regular continued fraction for √n.
